name: STAT3 loss-of-function (autosomal dominant hyper-IgE / Job syndrome)
aliases: signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 deficiency

clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant multisystem disorder caused by dominant-negative mutations in STAT3, classically presenting as the hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome

The immunological hallmark is a triad of recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses (often cold, lacking the usual warmth and inflammation), recurrent pneumonias with pneumatocoele formation, and a markedly elevated serum IgE
Chronic eczematoid dermatitis and mucocutaneous candidiasis are common and often begin in infancy
Connective-tissue and skeletal features are characteristic: a distinctive coarse facial appearance, hyperextensible joints, recurrent fractures with reduced bone density, and scoliosis
Retained primary teeth from failure of normal deciduous tooth shedding is a classic dental clue
Vascular abnormalities including aneurysm formation and tortuosity may develop, and pneumatocoeles can become secondarily infected with fungi such as aspergillus

Diagnosis integrates a clinical scoring approach with a high IgE, reduced interleukin-17-producing T cells, and confirmatory STAT3 sequencing; management centres on antistaphylococcal and antifungal prophylaxis, skin care, and vigilant treatment of lung complications
reference.pathophysiology: STAT3 is a transcription factor that relays signals from numerous cytokines, including interleukin-6, interleukin-10, interleukin-21, and interleukin-23. Dominant-negative mutations produce a protein that interferes with the normal STAT3 encoded by the intact allele, so STAT3-dependent signalling is broadly reduced. A key consequence is failure to generate interleukin-17-producing T-helper cells, which are needed to defend skin and mucosa against Staphylococcus aureus and candida, explaining the abscesses and candidiasis. Impaired STAT3 signalling also disturbs the regulation of inflammation (contributing to the paradoxically cold abscesses and elevated IgE), and because the same pathway participates in bone remodelling, connective-tissue maintenance, vascular integrity, and dental development, the disorder extends well beyond immunity into the skeletal, dental, and vascular abnormalities that define the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: DOCK8 deficiency autosomal recessive hyper-IgE syndrome
Severe atopic dermatitis with reactive IgE elevation
Chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent abscesses
Cystic fibrosis or other causes of recurrent pneumonia with cavitation
additionalInvestigations: Serum IgE with full blood count and eosinophil quantification
Quantitative immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses
Chest imaging to detect pneumatocoeles and monitor for secondary fungal infection
Bone density assessment and skeletal or dental review
Vascular imaging where aneurysm or tortuosity is suspected
redFlags: Recurrent cold staphylococcal abscesses with a very high IgE
Pneumatocoeles or cavitary lung disease with secondary aspergillus or other fungal infection
Aneurysm formation or coronary/cerebral vascular abnormality
reference.prognosis: Many patients survive into adulthood with attentive antimicrobial prophylaxis and skin care, but chronic lung damage with secondary fungal infection is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, and vascular and skeletal complications add to the long-term burden.
pitfalls: Mistaking cold abscesses for simple recurrent boils and missing the underlying syndrome
Draining or operating on pneumatocoeles without recognising the risk of secondary fungal colonisation and poor healing
Attributing a high IgE solely to atopy
Overlooking the non-immune skeletal, dental, and vascular features that aid diagnosis
Underusing antifungal and antistaphylococcal prophylaxis in established disease
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
